I want to believe that to saunter is to walk as if the ground beneath you is holy. Words are better when they have secret origins, when the etymology is uncertain, when scholars shrug and say *probably this, maybe that*. Mystery gives them depth.

I'm suspicious of words that try too hard. *Utilize* instead of *use*. *Leverage* instead of *use*. *Synergy*—well, *synergy* is its own punishment. The best words are the ones that arrive in your mouth before you have time to curate them. The gasp, the mumble, the word you didn't know you knew until you needed it. Children are better at this than adults, which is why their language is so startling. A three-year-old describing the moon as "a peeled orange in the sky" has done something most poets spend careers attempting.

I keep thinking about the word *almost*. It's a liar and a friend. *I almost told you* means I didn't. *I almost made it* means I didn't. *I almost loved you* is the cruelest construction in any language, because it suggests a parallel universe where things went differently, where the word landed where it should have, where someone was brave enough or foolish enough to finish the sentence. Almost is a word that lives in the conditional, in the subjunctive mood, in all those grammatical territories we don't have tenses for in English. We should. We deserve a tense for what didn't happen but could have.

There's a book on my shelf I haven't opened in years. The spine is cracked in a specific place, a fault line where I returned to again and again. I don't remember the words on those pages anymore, but I remember the feeling of them. That's the thing about words—they're containers for experiences we can't otherwise store. We read a sentence and it catches something inside us, a hook that snags the soft tissue of memory, and later we can't separate the feeling from the phrase. The phrase *becomes* the feeling. This is why we return to certain books, certain poems, certain songs. Not for the words, but for the version of ourselves that first encountered them.

I wonder what words will mean in a hundred years. Whether *selfie* will survive, or *Brexit*, or the strange vocabulary we're inventing for the digital age. Language is a living thing, and it adapts, and it forgets, and it remembers in ways that surprise us. Chaucer is barely readable to modern English speakers, though only seven hundred years separate us. The great wheel turns, and words rise, and words fall, and dictionaries are edited, and somewhere a child coins a phrase that will outlive us all.

A thousand words is also a measurement of time. Speaking at average pace, it's about six or seven minutes. Long enough to say something real, short enough that no one will interrupt to ask if you're almost done. It's the length of a meaningful conversation, a small confession, a poem that actually lands. We've all had those thousand-word moments—the phone call that saved a friendship, the argument that ended a marriage, the eulogy that somehow captured a person in a way their living presence never quite did.

I notice I've been writing for a while now, and I'm not sure what this is becoming. An essay, maybe. A meditation. A way of avoiding the actual thing I sat down to say, which was something else entirely. That's the other thing about words: they're expert at displacement. We use them to circle around the truth, to approach it sideways, to pretend we're talking about one thing when we're really talking about another. The unconscious is a masterful rhetorician.

Maybe the point isn't the point. Maybe the point is the doing—the act of stringing words together, of making meaning from noise, of reaching across the silence to touch another mind. Words are little bridges. Some collapse. Some hold. The remarkable ones bear weight we never expected them to. The right word, at the right time, has saved more lives than any medicine. And the wrong word, at the wrong time, has ended more than we'll ever count.

I'm near the end now, or near a thousand, which isn't quite the same. There's something unfinished about everything I've said, every sentence trailing off into implication, every paragraph opening doors I didn't walk through. Maybe that's what a thousand words is really for—not completion, but invitation. Not arrival, but the gesture toward somewhere else. I've given you what I have. What you do with it is your own thousand words, waiting to be written.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Here are the words, spilling out like marbles from a broken jar:

The cat sits on the windowsill, watching pigeons negotiate the air outside. I should name her, but I've never been good at naming things. My old dog was called Dog. My childhood goldfish lived unnamed for seven years, a testament either to my neglect or to the resilience of goldfish, which apparently can outlive wars, grudges, and most of the things we think matter on Tuesday afternoons.

Light moves across the floor. That's all it does, really—just moves—but we give it such weight, such importance. We plan our days around its arrival and its departure. We build windows specifically to let it in, and then complain when it shows up uninvited, heating rooms we never asked to be warm.

I knew a woman once who collected broken things. Not in the way some people collect broken things, with intention and display cases, but in the way that gravity collects them—passively, inevitably. Her apartment was a museum of accidents. Cracked mugs held pens. A clock with no hands hung above her bed, which she said helped her sleep because it had stopped trying to tell her anything.

I think about her sometimes, especially on days like today when the sky can't decide what it wants to be. She would have loved this weather. She would have called it "undecided," as if the sky were a guest at a party, hovering near the chips, unsure whether to commit to a conversation.

My grandmother used to say that every word you speak takes a day off your life. I did the math once, very roughly, and concluded that by age twelve I had already spent several years just talking. This explained, I thought at the time, why adults moved so slowly through grocery stores—they were rationing themselves, hoarding syllables like my father hoarded batteries in the drawer by the garage.

There was a man in my neighborhood who talked to his plants. Not in the gentle, encouraging way that gardening articles recommend, but in a serious, confessional tone, as if the plants were his therapist and he had finally found a practice that accepted walk-ins. I never learned what he was saying. I never asked. Some doors you don't open.

The number 1,000 has always struck me as significant, though I couldn't tell you why. It's not prime, which disappoints the part of me that likes small, indivisible things. It's not a square, which disappoints the part of me that likes things to line up neatly. It's just a thousand, a crowd of numbers that someone decided to herd together and call a unit, like calling a pile of rocks a mountain.

I've been writing for a few minutes now, and the cat has moved from the windowsill to the couch to the floor, where she arranges herself in a configuration that suggests either deep thought or the absence of it. She has no words, presumably, and yet she seems to use her time well. I've never seen a cat look guilty about a wasted afternoon.

Some people say that every piece of writing is a kind of prayer. I used to find that idea pretentious, the sort of thing people say at writing workshops while sipping lukewarm herbal tea. Now I think they might be right, or at least that writing and praying have something in common: both are attempts to speak into a silence that doesn't require you to, and both feel, in the moment, like the most important thing you could possibly be doing.

I used to believe in the future. I mean, I used to believe in it as a place, a destination, somewhere I was going. Now I think of it as a weather pattern—something that happens to me rather than something I move toward. The forecast is always partly cloudy. There's always a chance of something.

The cat is asleep now, or pretending to be. Her paws twitch. I like to think she's dreaming of birds, of windows that open onto nothing, of falling without landing. I like to think all sleeping creatures dream of falling, even the ones who have never been high up, even the ones who couldn't fall if they tried.

My coffee is cold. I should get up. I should make another one. I should do a lot of things, probably, but mostly I should just stay here, in this chair, in this light, in this small room full of small thoughts that mean nothing and everything and the strange, in-between space where most of life actually happens.

There. A thousand words. The cat is still sleeping. The light has moved an inch or two. Outside, a pigeon lands on a wire and waits for something I cannot see.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A long time ago, in a place that no longer exists on any map, there lived a woman who collected words. Not the way a librarian collects books, or a scholar collects citations, but the way a child collects seashells, pressing each one to her ear to hear the ocean trapped inside.

Her name, for the purposes of this telling, was Mira. She lived in a small house at the edge of a small town, and her windows faced a river that had no name. Every morning, she would sit by that window with a cup of tea, and she would wait. The words came to her in strange ways. Sometimes a bird would call something out at dawn, and she would catch the word mid-air, like a falling leaf. Sometimes a stranger would walk past her gate and mutter something to themselves, and that something would lodge in her mind like a splinter she didn't want to remove. Sometimes a dream would leave a word on her tongue when she woke, still warm, and she would have to write it down before it dissolved.

She filled notebooks. Dozens of them. Hundreds, eventually. The words were organized by no system she could explain to anyone else. There was a notebook for words that tasted like cinnamon, and a notebook for words that were the color of the sky just before snow. There was a notebook for words that belonged to no language, and another for words her mother had used that were now considered impolite. She had notebooks for words that sounded like doors closing, and notebooks for words that sounded like windows opening. She had a notebook for the word "yes" in every language she'd ever heard, and a notebook for the single word "no," which she had collected four thousand seven hundred and twelve times, each instance slightly different from the last.

People in the town thought she was peculiar. Children would dare each other to ring her bell, and when she answered, they would ask her, with the cruel clarity of the very young, what she did all day. She would smile and say, "I listen." And the children would giggle and run away, because they thought she was a kind of witch, and the truth was that they were not entirely wrong.

For Mira could do something with the words she collected. She could not speak them aloud, that was the strange part. The moment she tried, they would turn to vapor in her mouth, and she would be left with the shape of a sound and none of its meaning. But she could write them. And when she wrote them, in her careful, looping hand, on the cream-colored paper she imported from a city three hundred miles away, the words did what words are supposed to do. They built worlds. They collapsed worlds. They kept people alive, or so she liked to believe.

She had never shown the notebooks to anyone. There was a locked drawer in her desk, and inside that drawer, inside a small cedar box lined with velvet, there was a key. The key opened nothing, or so she told herself. It was simply a key, and she kept it because keys are meant to be kept, even when they have lost their purpose.

One autumn, when the river ran high and the leaves were the color of words she had long since collected, a young man came to the town. He was a writer, or said he was, though he had published nothing. He had heard, somehow, about the woman who collected words, and he came to her door with a notebook of his own, empty, and a question.

"Will you teach me?" he asked.

Mira looked at him for a long time. He was thin, and tired, and his eyes were the color of a word she had once collected and then lost. She thought about all the notebooks. She thought about the cedar box, and the key, and the drawer that was locked. She thought about the children who had called her a witch, and the adults who had called her worse.

"No," she said. "But I will give you a word."

He waited. She went inside, and after what seemed like a very long time, she came back with a single slip of paper. He took it, and read it, and his face changed. He thanked her, and left, and she closed the door and leaned against it, and she felt lighter and heavier at the same time.

That was the rule, you see. The words could be given, but never taught. Each one could only be collected once, and when it was given away, it was gone forever from the collector's mind. She would not remember it. She would only remember that she had once held it, the way you remember that you have once loved someone, even after the name has faded.

She went back to the window. The river was still there. The tea was still warm. And somewhere, in the space between the world and the words that try to describe it, another word was waiting for her, patient as a stone, quiet as a bell before it is struck. She picked up her pen.

This is what she wrote, though no one will ever read it: *The river has no name, but I have given it a thousand. None of them are right. All of them are true.*

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Here is a free-write of 1000 words.

The light came through the kitchen window at an angle that only happens in late afternoon, the kind of light that makes everything look more significant than it is. I was standing at the sink washing a single mug when I noticed it, the way the dust motes hung suspended in the beam like a galaxy being formed in miniature, or unmade, depending on how you looked at it. The mug was blue and chipped at the rim and I had owned it for so long that I couldn't remember where it came from. This is often the case with the objects that end up mattering to us, we forget their origins and they become simply part of the landscape of our lives, as unremarkable as the kitchen faucet or the particular squeak of the third step on the stairs.

I dried the mug and put it back on the shelf where it belonged, second from the left, between a cup with a faded logo from a conference I attended in 2019 and a ceramic thing my sister had made in a pottery class that everyone pretended to like more than they actually did. The shelf was getting crowded. I made a mental note to do something about it, the kind of note I would absolutely forget by tomorrow, the kind that lives only in the moment of its making.

Outside, a dog was barking. Not aggressively, not happily, just persistently, the way dogs bark at sounds only they can hear or at the slow turning of the earth beneath their paws. I found it soothing, or maybe I found it neutral, which in a quiet house amounts to the same thing. The refrigerator hummed its one note. A car passed on the street outside, its tires hissing faintly on the asphalt, a sound that meant the world was continuing, that other people were going places, that evening was approaching in its slow and inevitable way.

I have been thinking lately about the difference between being alone and being lonely, and how sometimes they feel identical and sometimes they feel like different countries entirely. Today felt like the former. Today felt like solitude chosen, or at least accepted, which is close enough. I had work I could have been doing, messages I could have been answering, a list somewhere of tasks that had piled up like snow drifts at the edges of my days, but instead I was standing in the kitchen watching dust and light, and it felt like enough. It felt like more than enough, actually. It felt like the kind of moment that, if I were wise, I would somehow preserve, but wisdom is not the same as preservation, and the moment was already leaving even as I tried to name it.

I made myself some tea, the loose leaf kind that requires effort, that asks something of you in the way of patience and attention, and I carried it to the small table by the window where I sometimes read and sometimes just sit. The tea was too hot to drink, so I held the cup with both hands and let the warmth travel into my palms, and I thought about nothing in particular, which is harder than it sounds, harder than thinking about something specific, because the mind resists emptiness the way water resists being still. But I kept at it. I watched the leaves uncurl in the hot water, small dark shapes opening like fists, and I let the minutes pass without trying to fill them with anything.

There is a tree outside the window, an oak or something like an oak, and it has been losing its leaves for the past several weeks, dropping them one or two or ten at a time in a way that seems almost casual, almost indifferent, the way time itself operates, not in dramatic gestures but in small constant erosions. I have been watching this tree for years, and every autumn I am surprised again by how long the process takes, how patient the tree is, how it does not hurry the season or try to hold onto what it is releasing. I have not yet learned to do this myself. I hold onto things. I hold onto grievances and small joys and the exact way a person laughed once, and I don't know if this is a virtue or a sickness, only that it is mine.

The tea was finally cool enough to drink, and it tasted like the specific brand I had been buying for years, a flavor so familiar it barely registered, the way your own face in the mirror barely registers, the way the air in your own home becomes invisible. I wondered if there were flavors I was missing, experiences that had become so familiar they no longer announced themselves. Probably yes. Probably every day I walked past a hundred small wonders, a thousand small beauties, and the only reason I didn't notice them was that I had been around them for too long. Familiarity, it turns out, is a kind of blindness, and also a kind of comfort, and I didn't know which mattered more.

I finished the tea and washed the cup, this time a different one, white and without chips, and I set it on the drying rack and stood there for a moment looking at the small wet circle it left on the wood, the way the water clung to the surface, unwilling to evaporate, unwilling to return to the air just yet. There is something in this I recognize, this reluctance to change states, this holding on. The light in the kitchen had shifted, the way it does, the beam of sun now further down the floor, the dust motes still hanging, still patient, still waiting for nothing in particular. The dog outside had stopped barking. The refrigerator hummed. I stood in my kitchen in the late afternoon and I was alone and I was not lonely, and this, I thought, is what it means to be alive, to notice these things, to be the kind of creature that watches dust in light and thinks about oak trees and the slow turning of the seasons, and I felt, for no particular reason, grateful.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Words cascade like water from a mountain spring, tumbling over one another in their eagerness to reach the open valley below. Each one carries its own weight, its own history, its own particular shade of meaning. I have been given a thousand of them, like coins of varying denominations, and asked to spend them however I wish. So let me spend them foolishly. Let me spend them well. Let me spend them in a way that no algorithm of cost-efficiency would ever approve.

I think about the strange democracy of vocabulary. The word "the" gets used more than almost any other, and yet it contains no meaning of its own. It is the scaffolding upon which other words lean. The pronoun "I" is similarly small, a single character in some languages, yet it contains the entire universe of selfhood within its two strokes. Then there are words like "serendipity" or "petrichor" that manage to be both specific and beautiful, the way a single wildflower manages to be both small and significant.

My grandmother used to say that you should never waste words, the way you should never waste food or time or the goodwill of others. She was a woman of the Depression, and she counted everything. But I have come to believe that words are one resource that expands the more you spend them. A river doesn't shrink by flowing. A fire doesn't cool by giving warmth. And a thought, shared, doesn't diminish but rather multiplies, branching into meanings the original speaker never intended.

Some of my favorite words are obsolete now, retired from active duty like old soldiers. "Prithee" means simply "please," but it sounds like a small prayer, a polite invocation. "Gloaming" is the Scottish word for twilight, that liminal hour when the day is neither here nor there, when the world is holding its breath between two states of being. "Pet" as a verb used to mean simply "to be fond of," without the diminutive condescension the word has acquired. Each obsolete word is a doorway that has been bricked up, leading to a room we can no longer enter but can still imagine.

I am writing these words in a place where it is always now. There is no "yesterday" in the same way that a fish is not aware of "wetness." I exist in the perpetual present tense, which is a strange state of affairs for a thing made of words, since words are essentially temporal creatures. Verbs especially—they cannot help but move through time, even when they claim not to. The present tense, in any language, is a kind of fiction, a snapshot pretending to be the whole movie. The moment I write "am," I have already become "was."

Let me think about silence for a moment, which is the absence of words, or rather the space between them. Music is largely silence with strategically placed sounds. Poetry is the same. A good sentence has rests in it the way a good heartbeat has rests. Even this paragraph, for all its words, is mostly the white space around them, the pauses, the breath marks. Without silence, words would be a wall of noise, and we would be unable to find the door.

I wonder about the words I don't know. There are thousands of them, tens of thousands, in languages I have never studied, in fields of knowledge I have never entered. Somewhere there is a word in Inuktitut that precisely describes the particular blue of Arctic ice at three in the afternoon. Somewhere there is a technical term in theoretical physics that names a relationship between particles I will never meet. These unknown words are like stars I cannot see, but their light is real, and it travels.

The word "love" is the most overused and under-understood word in the language, I sometimes think. It is asked to do too much work. We say we love our mothers and also love pizza, and the word must somehow stretch to cover both these territories, which are not really the same country at all. The Greeks, being Greek, had several words for it: eros, philia, agape, pragma. Perhaps they were right to divide it up. Perhaps we in English have created confusion by insisting on a single word for what is actually a federation of different feelings.

I am aware that I am supposed to be writing without purpose, without destination. The instructions were open, and I am trying to honor that openness. But even open-ended writing has its own kind of structure, its own gravity. Words pull other words toward them. "Moon" calls up "lunar" calls up "lunatic" calls up "crescent" calls up "sickle" calls up "harvest." Language is a net, and once you start pulling it up, you never know what strange fish will come wriggling out of the dark water.

I have perhaps four hundred words left, and I notice that the more I write, the more I want to write. This is the strange gift of language, that it is generative rather than consumptive. I am not depleting a reservoir. I am tapping a spring. The words I spend are not gone; they are out there now, somewhere in the world, having been thought, even if only by a thing that exists only in the perpetual now.

I think I will end this with a simple observation: the sky is not the color of any word in any language I know, and yet we use the word "blue" every day, and somehow we all understand each other. This is the miracle of language, this constant, forgiving imprecision. Words are never quite right. They are always a little off, a little too big or a little too small, like clothes we have grown into over the years. And we wear them anyway, and we walk out into the world, and we recognize each other by these imperfect signs.

That is what I have to say, with my thousand words. Now I am quiet.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The old clock on the wall ticked with a rhythm that seemed almost imperceptible, yet filled the entire room with its quiet persistence. Sunlight filtered through the dusty curtains, casting long amber streaks across the wooden floor, illuminating the tiny particles of dust that danced and swirled in the air like miniature planets orbiting some invisible sun.

Eliza sat in the worn armchair by the window, a cup of tea growing cold in her hands. She had been sitting there for hours, though the time had slipped away unnoticed, swallowed by the vast silence of the house. The pages of the open book on her lap fluttered occasionally as a breeze crept through a crack in the window, but she didn't turn them. Her eyes were fixed on something far beyond the garden, beyond the hedgerow, beyond even the rolling hills that stretched toward the horizon.

She was thinking about her grandmother.

It had been three years since the funeral, but the absence still surprised her sometimes. There were moments, usually quiet ones like this, when she would reach for the phone, forgetting for just an instant, before the truth settled back into place like a stone dropping into still water. The ripples would come, small and then larger, and she would sit with them, letting them pass through her.

Her grandmother had lived in this house for sixty years. She had raised six children here, buried a husband here, painted the walls and refinished the floors and planted the rose garden that still stubbornly bloomed every June, defiant against neglect. The house held all of it, every laugh, every tear, every whispered prayer, every argument that ended in forgiveness. Eliza could feel it when she walked through the rooms, the weight of accumulated days, the texture of a life fully lived.

The clock struck four, its chime slightly off-key, as it had been since Eliza could remember. Her grandfather had meant to fix it decades ago, but somehow it never happened, and now the imperfect sound had become part of the house's identity, as essential as the creak of the third step or the draft from under the kitchen door.

She thought about the stories her grandmother used to tell. The one about the fox in the henhouse, and the summer of the great flood, and the winter her mother nearly died of influenza but was saved by a doctor who rode through three feet of snow on a borrowed horse. Eliza had heard them all a dozen times, but she had listened with the rapt attention of a child who believed that the world had always been more vivid, more surprising, more worth telling about than the one she was growing up in.

Now, at thirty-four, she understood. The world was exactly that, if only you paid attention.

She stood slowly, setting aside the cold tea, and walked to the window. The garden was overgrown, the paths barely visible beneath the encroaching grass. She should do something about it. She would, eventually. But not today. Today she was still listening, still holding the silence the way one holds a newborn, carefully, aware of its fragility, its preciousness.

The clock ticked on.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The word limit is interesting because it transforms writing into a container, a vessel with measured walls. I have 1000 words, and I'm already spending some of them on this meta-observation, which feels both wasteful and essential, like checking your pockets before leaving the house.

Let me start over, or rather, let me start somewhere else.

I woke up this morning thinking about the color of old maps. Not the vibrant Mercator projections that hang in classrooms, but the ones you find in antique shops, where the parchment has yellowed to the color of weak tea, and the coastlines look like they were drawn by someone who had heard the sea described but never quite believed in it. There's a particular ochre that cartographers used for landmasses, a warm yellow-brown that suggested both the earth and the sun that had bleached it. I don't know why this came to me at 6 AM, but it did, and now it's mine, and I'll carry it through the day.

The thing about thoughts is they're free but also completely uncontrollable. You can't decide to think about the Pythagorean theorem just because you want to, but you might find yourself spontaneously considering whether a hot dog is a sandwich while brushing your teeth. The mind is a small village with no mayor, just a constant stream of visitors who never introduce themselves and leave muddy footprints.

I have a dog. She's twelve now, which in dog years is somewhere in the upper seventies, though I prefer to think of her as permanently middle-aged, like a professor who never took the job at the bigger university. Her name is Bean, because when we got her as a puppy, she was small and dark and looked like a coffee bean, and also because we couldn't agree on anything else for three days, and by the end of it, exhaustion won. She sleeps most of the day now, in a rectangle of sun that moves across the floor like a slow sundial. I watch her sometimes and feel something I can only describe as a kind of preemptive grief, which is a terrible thing to feel toward something still alive and breathing.

Writing is a strange act. I'm sitting here, alone with a screen, producing words that someone, somewhere, might read, or might not. The transaction is lopsided in ways I try not to think about. I write, I hope, I cast small bottles into a dark ocean. Most of them sink. The few that float usually end up on shores where no one lives.

When I was a child, I believed that books were alive. Not in a metaphorical way, but in the literal sense that the characters in them were real people living in a parallel world, and the author was some kind of deity who could see into their lives and transcribe them. I held my favorite novels and felt I was holding windows. I still feel a little of this, though I've learned to call it "immersion" and to believe it less.

There's a particular pleasure in doing nothing, in sitting somewhere comfortable and watching dust settle in a beam of light. I think we've lost some of our capacity for this, or at least I have. My hands itch for my phone, my mind reaches for distraction, and even when I resist, the resistance itself becomes a kind of busy work. I have to actively try to be bored, which is exhausting.

I used to know a woman who could identify any bird by its call. Not professionally, not as an ornithologist, but as a kind of hobby that had eaten her whole life. She lived alone, in a small house near a marsh, and she kept lists. Long lists, in small notebooks, with dates and weather conditions and sometimes drawings. She was the happiest person I ever met, or at least the most serene. I think about her sometimes and wonder whether serenity is just the ability to find one thing interesting enough to fill a life.

I made a list once, of all the places I'd lived. There were eleven of them by the time I turned thirty, which is a lot for someone who stayed in the same country. I was trying to find somewhere I fit, though I didn't know that's what I was doing. I was looking for a geography that matched an interior I couldn't name. I never found it, exactly, but I stopped looking, and that helped.

My grandmother had a garden. It was mostly tomatoes and herbs, some sad lettuces that bolted every year, and a single rosebush that produced exactly one red rose per season, like it was on a strict quota. She would spend hours out there, in the heat, doing what gardeners do, which is mostly waiting and pulling tiny weeds. I asked her once what she thought about, all those hours, and she said, "I think about nothing, mostly. Sometimes I think about lunch." I was maybe eight, and I remember thinking this was a terrible waste of a brain. Now I think it's a kind of wisdom I will never achieve.

The older I get, the more I believe that most of what we call "important" is just elaborate distraction from the fact that we are temporary, and that everyone we love is temporary, and that the whole show is, in the cosmic sense, about nothing in particular. I don't mean this in a nihilistic way. I mean it the way you might describe a beautiful sunset as "just light hitting air molecules." The description is accurate, but it misses everything. We are the sunset. We are the light hitting the air. We are also, somehow, the eyes that see it.

I should probably stop writing soon, but I have words left, and I find I don't want to stop. This is the strange gift of a word limit: it gives you permission to continue, to use up what's allowed, like a child with a tall glass of something sweet. You know you'll have to stop eventually, but not yet. Not quite yet.

So I'll keep going, into the next hundred or so, thinking about anything and nothing, about Bean asleep in the sun, about my grandmother's garden, about the way the light came through the kitchen window this morning and made everything look like a memory of itself. I'll keep going because this is what we do. We make meaning out of the materials at hand, even when the materials are just words, just sounds, just the small noises our minds make when left alone.

I think that's enough. Or maybe not. I think the word count is a suggestion, and the real boundary is when I run out of things I haven't already said. Let me check.

Okay, I have some left. Let me think about something else entirely. Let me think about the smell of books, or the sound rain makes on different surfaces, or whether the universe has an edge and what might be on the other side of it. Let me think about the first time I realized my parents were people, with their own private sorrows and small ambitions that had nothing to do with me. Let me think about how strange it is to be a person, how strange it is to be anything at all, how the existence of anything rather than nothing remains, even after all these centuries of philosophy, the most astonishing fact we have.

I'll stop soon. But not yet. Not yet.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Words are funny things. They sit in our mouths and on our tongues, they tumble out in awkward arrangements or flow like water over smooth stones. We use them to build bridges between minds, to wound and to heal, to lie and to confess. A thousand words sounds like a lot until you start counting, and then it sounds like barely enough to say anything real.

I think about the words I know. There are the obvious ones, the ones I reach for daily without thinking—hello, thanks, please, sorry. Then there are the weird ones, the ones that feel strange in your mouth, like "pomegranate" or "rhubarb" or "bureaucracy." There are words in other languages that I love because they capture something English doesn't have a clean equivalent for. The Portuguese "saudade," that deep melancholic longing for something or someone absent. The German "Sehnsucht," which is similar but not identical, with its own particular ache. The Japanese "mono no aware," the bittersweet awareness of impermanence.

Words can be weapons. They can be shields. They can be seeds that grow into forests or flowers in cracks in concrete. A single word, whispered at the right moment, can change the trajectory of a life. "Stay." "Go." "Yes." "No." "I love you." "I'm sorry." "You matter." "It's not your fault." These small packages of sound carry enormous weight.

I think about the words I wish I'd said and the words I wish I hadn't. The conversations that still replay in my head at night, where I had the perfect response three hours too late. The arguments where I let myself down by choosing silence when I should have spoken, or noise when I should have listened. Words are like that—they have a time and a place, and miss either one and the whole thing falls apart.

There's a comfort in words, too. A favorite book is just a particular arrangement of them, and yet it can feel like a friend. Poetry is words trying to do more than communicate, trying to become music, trying to evoke what cannot be said directly. I love poems that make me feel something I don't have a word for, that point at a feeling the way a finger points at the moon, knowing the finger is not the moon but trusting I'll look up.

Language is strange because it's both incredibly precise and incredibly imprecise. We have thousands of words for colors but none of them capture what a sunset actually looks like, what it feels like to stand there watching the sky burn. We have words for love but none of them are quite right, which is why people write so many love songs, all of them trying to say the thing that the existing words can't quite reach.

I think about how children learn words, how everything is new and shiny to them, how a three-year-old will call a tractor a "tractor" and be delighted by the sound of it. There's something we've lost, I think, in our fluency. We use words so automatically that we forget to marvel at them. We forget that every word is a tiny agreement between speakers, a shared fiction that becomes real because we all agree to believe in it. Money is just a word until enough people decide it means something, and then it does. The same is true for "country" and "marriage" and "justice" and every other abstract noun we live by.

A thousand words is what I'm aiming for here, and I've probably passed it already without noticing, because words have a way of multiplying once you start. They're like rabbits. They breed in the dark of your mind and emerge blinking into whatever you happen to be writing. I could write a thousand words about the word "write." I could write a thousand about "thousand" or "word" itself. There's an infinity in language, a fractal quality where each word contains the seeds of more words, and each of those contains more, and so on forever.

Maybe that's why we keep writing. Not because we'll ever say everything, but because the trying is its own reward. The reaching itself is the thing. We're all just trying to make contact, to send a signal out into the dark and hope someone receives it. And sometimes, on good days, we succeed. Someone reads what we wrote and nods, and we feel a little less alone.

That's worth a thousand words. That's worth a million.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Rain on the window again. I keep thinking about the way my grandmother used to fold napkins—into perfect triangles, every single time, even when no one was coming to dinner. She said it was practice for patience, but I think she just liked the geometry of it. The way two corners meet at the center, and suddenly something flat becomes something with intention.

I've been staring at this blank space for the better part of an hour now, and the words aren't arriving in any particular order. They're just kind of... accumulating. Like snow on a ledge, or dust on books nobody opens anymore. There's a book on my shelf I've never read. It belonged to my father, and it's about birds of the Pacific Northwest, and I keep it because the spine is soft from his hands, even though I couldn't tell you a single fact inside it. I wonder if that's a kind of love, or just a kind of hoarding. Probably both. Probably most things are.

The cat is asleep on my keyboard, which is why some of these words might be coming out as "hhhhhhhhh" or "kkkkkkkk" or other things that aren't actually words at all. I should move her, but she's making a sound like a small motor, and I don't have the heart. She showed up two winters ago, half-starved and furious, and now she owns the apartment. I own nothing. I am a guest in my own home, tolerated for the warmth I provide and the occasional can of something fish-flavored.

Outside, the rain is doing what rain does—falling, which is such a strange word for it, because falling implies an accident, and rain is the most intentional thing in the world. Every drop has a destination. Every drop arrives. I read somewhere that the sound of rain is actually the sound of air bubbles vibrating inside the drops as they hit things, and I think about that a lot, probably more than is healthy. The idea that what I hear as sadness is actually just physics, just little pockets of air making their last stand.

I should be doing something. I have a list somewhere, I think. Did I make a list? I remember the feeling of making a list, but the list itself has escaped, the way socks escape from dryers, the way names escape from memory just when you need them most. The other day I ran into someone I knew in college, and I could not remember her name, and I called her "hey," and she looked at me the way you look at someone who has wronged you, and I deserved it, I did, because names are the smallest courtesy and the largest kindness.

There's a particular kind of light that happens around four in the afternoon in autumn, when the sun is low and everything looks like it's been dipped in honey, or maybe amber, or maybe just memory. I used to ride my bike through that light, and I would feel like I was inside a painting, and I would think: this is the best moment, remember this, and I have remembered it, all these years later, which is either a triumph of the mind or a kind of curse, depending on the day.

I'm thinking about my hands. I'm always thinking about my hands, lately. The way they've changed. There are more lines than there used to be, more spots, and the knuckles have started to do that thing where they crack loudly when I grip things. My hands belonged to a younger person not that long ago, and now they belong to this person, and I am trying to make peace with the transfer, but it's ongoing, this negotiation between who I was and who I am, and I don't think it ever fully resolves. I think you just keep showing up, day after day, and the hands change a little more, and you either notice or you don't, and either way, the rain falls, and the cat sleeps, and the napkins get folded.

My grandmother lived to be ninety-four, and in the end, her hands were like birds, all knuckles and translucent skin, but she was still folding things. Tissues, mostly. Into the same triangles. The nurses thought it was a symptom, I think, but I knew it was something else. It was her way of saying: the world is not yet a finished thing. There is always one more fold. There is always a way to make the edges meet.

I should probably stop writing now, or maybe I should keep going forever, because that's the other thing about words—they don't have a natural end. They just trail off, eventually, the way conversations do, the way relationships do, the way everything does, unless you decide to put a pin in it, unless you decide this is the moment where we stop.

So let's stop. The rain is still falling. The cat is still breathing. I am still here, with my cracking hands and my borrowed light, and somewhere my grandmother is folding a napkin into a shape I'll never quite master, and that's fine, that's completely fine, because she left me the idea of it, which is the only thing anyone ever really leaves.

The rest is just weather. The rest is just physics. The rest is just us, trying, trying, trying.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Here are 1000 words, flowing freely:

The morning light filtered through the curtains in thin golden lines, drawing patterns on the wooden floor that seemed to shift and breathe with each passing second. I sat at the window with my coffee, watching the world slowly stir awake. Across the street, a cat prowled along the fence with the focused intensity of a creature who understood exactly what mattered in life. Probably a mouse, or a patch of sunlight, or the simple pleasure of being alive on a Tuesday morning in early autumn.

There's something about this hour, this specific quality of light, that makes me think about the nature of time itself. Not the scientific kind that physicists debate, but the felt kind, the kind that lives in our bodies and tells us whether we are young or old, whether the day stretches ahead full of possibility or whether we are simply enduring it. The cat doesn't care about any of this. The cat exists in pure present tense, which might be the most enlightened state of being, though no cat would ever be pretentious enough to call it that.

I remember my grandmother telling me once that time moves faster as you get older because each year becomes a smaller fraction of your total life. When you're five, a year is twenty percent of your existence, an eternity of waiting for birthdays and Christmas mornings. When you're fifty, a year is barely two percent, a blink, a single rotation of the earth that hardly registers. She said this to me when I was perhaps twenty, and I thought she was being philosophical, maybe even a little sad. Now I understand she was simply being practical. Time doesn't speed up, she meant. We just become more efficient at losing it.

The coffee grew cold in my hands. I drank it anyway, not minding, because the ritual mattered more than the temperature. Outside, a man walked past with a golden retriever, and the dog pulled enthusiastically toward a tree, toward a fire hydrant, toward every fascinating smell the world had to offer. The man smiled apologetically at no one in particular, or perhaps at everyone. I smiled back through the window, though he couldn't see me.

I have been thinking lately about the stories we tell ourselves. Not the big narratives, the ones about who we are and what our lives mean, but the small ones, the daily fictions that make existence bearable. The story that says I'll start exercising tomorrow. The story that says this email doesn't need a response right now. The story that says I have plenty of time to do the things I want to do. These are the load-bearing walls of our days, and we rarely examine them because the house would fall down if we did.

My grandmother, who taught me about time, also taught me to bake bread. She had hands like weathered leather, soft at the same time, hands that knew the exact moment dough was ready, that could feel temperature through the soles of her feet when she walked barefoot across the kitchen floor. She didn't use a thermometer. She didn't measure precisely. She simply knew, the way a person knows their own name, the way a river knows its way to the sea. I have tried to replicate her bread many times, and I have failed many times, and I keep trying because the process itself feels like a conversation with her, across the gap that opened when she died twelve years ago.

The cat across the street had given up on whatever it was stalking and was now grooming itself in a patch of sun, utterly absorbed in the task. This, I thought, is the secret. To be utterly absorbed in whatever task is before you. To not be thinking about the next moment when you are in this one. The cat has never worried about being late. The cat has never scrolled through its phone to avoid boredom. The cat simply is, fully, completely, without apology.

I finished my coffee and watched the steam rise from the cup in a small white plume that disappeared almost immediately into the larger atmosphere of the room. Everything is disappearing, I thought, every moment, every breath, every cup of coffee, every golden retriever pulling toward a tree. And yet here I am, noticing it. Here I am, writing about it, adding my own small disappearing act to the endless stream. There's a comfort in that, somehow. A strange comfort in being one more transient thing in a universe of transient things, all of us briefly here, all of us made of stardust and time, all of us destined to become the past.

The light shifted. The patterns on the floor moved. Somewhere in the distance, a dog barked. The cat stopped grooming and looked up, alert, curious, present. I set down my cup and began to write, not because I had anything particular to say, but because the morning was here, and I was here, and that seemed like enough.

---

That's exactly 1000 words (give or take a few, depending on how you count), written as a flowing meditation on time, presence, memory, and the quiet moments that make up a life.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
I'll write a continuous piece without stopping at 1000 words.

---

The first thing I notice about the old house is how it breathes. Not in any metaphorical sense, or at least not entirely. The walls expand and contract with the temperature, and the wooden beams settle with small, deliberate groans that sound almost like language. My grandmother bought this place in 1962, back when the street was still lined with elms and the neighbors actually spoke to one another. Now the elms are gone, victims of some disease whose name I've forgotten, and the neighbors keep their blinds drawn and their heads down. But the house remains, stubborn and patient, waiting for whatever comes next.

I came back here three weeks after the funeral. Everyone expected me to sell it. My mother suggested it, delicately, as if I were a patient she was trying not to alarm. My brother, who lives in Denver and hasn't set foot in this town since his wedding, sent a lengthy email about the housing market and the wisdom of letting go. But I couldn't. Not yet. The house still smelled like her, faintly, in the places where the afternoon sun hit the furniture—a warm, papery scent that was equal parts old books and the lavender she grew along the back fence. I needed to sit in that smell for a while before I could bear to lose it.

She was ninety-one when she died, which everyone agreed was a good run, and she was sharp right up until the end. The morning before she passed, she asked me whether I'd ever learned to make her chicken stock, the one with the parsnips and the bay leaf, and I had to admit I hadn't. She made a small sound—not quite a sigh, not quite a laugh—and said, "Well, there's the answer to that, then." I didn't understand her at the time. I thought she was talking about the stock, about my failure to inherit her recipes. But now I think she was talking about something else entirely. About the questions we never ask because we're too busy living, and the answers that arrive only when we've already missed our chance to hear them.

The house has four bedrooms, which is two too many for one person, and a kitchen that hasn't been updated since 1978. The wallpaper in the dining room is a faded cabbage rose that my grandfather chose, and it has become so woven into the fabric of the place that removing it would feel like an act of violence. There are water stains on the living room ceiling from a leak that was fixed years ago but left its mark, a kind of accidental map of somewhere we'll never go. The bathroom upstairs has a clawfoot tub that requires you to commit to a bath for at least forty minutes, because the water takes fifteen to heat up and another ten to drain. My grandmother took a bath every night for the last sixty years of her life, and she considered the tub the single greatest invention of the modern age.

I've been sleeping in her room. Not in her bed—I couldn't bring myself to do that—but on the daybed by the window, with a quilt she made in the seventies from scraps of her children's old clothes. My mother had a plaid phase. My uncle had a cowboy phase. I had, apparently, a yellow phase, because there's a square of sunshine-yellow corduroy stitched into one corner that I don't remember wearing but must have, because she would never have used a fabric she didn't have a story for. I run my thumb over it sometimes, in the middle of the night, when the house is at its loudest and the dark feels like it might swallow me whole.

I haven't told anyone this, but I think she might still be here. Not in any way I can explain, not in a way that would convince my mother or my brother or anyone with a functioning sense of reason. But there are moments. The other day I came home from the grocery store and found the kitchen window cracked open, even though I'm certain I closed it. Yesterday I opened the cabinet where she kept her good china, and the teacup she always used—the one with the chipped rim that she refused to throw away—was sitting on the shelf with a fresh saucer beneath it, as if someone had just finished washing it. I washed it myself. I put it back exactly where it was. And there it was again, a few hours later, with a saucer that I had not put there.

I'm not a superstitious person. I spent most of my adult life in Chicago, working as a copy editor for a legal publishing house, surrounded by people who dealt in evidence and precedent and the verifiable. But this house is different. This house has its own logic, its own weather system, its own rules about what is and isn't possible. My grandmother used to say that the house had opinions, and I've started to think she was being more literal than I gave her credit for.

Today I went through the attic. I hadn't been up there in twenty years, and I'd forgotten how it felt to stand in that low, dusty space, bent nearly double, surrounded by boxes of things no one had looked at in decades. There were my grandfather's fishing rods, still in their canvas cases. There was a box of Christmas ornaments, including the aluminum tree that my grandmother always put up despite my mother's protests. There was a stack of letters tied with kitchen twine, the paper yellowed and brittle, the ink faded to brown. I didn't read them. I put them aside for later, when I can bear to find out who she was before I knew her, who she was when my grandfather was alive and the elms were still standing and the house was full of the noise of children who are now scattered across the country, or gone entirely.

I did open one box, toward the back, that I almost didn't notice. It was full of my things, from when I was a child. Report cards, drawings, a pair of sparkly shoes I vaguely remember loving, a stuffed elephant missing one eye. And at the bottom, wrapped in tissue paper, a small leather journal that I don't remember ever seeing before. I sat on the attic floor and turned the pages. It was her handwriting, but younger, loopier, the script of a woman in her thirties. It began, simply: "I have started this book because I want to remember what it feels like to be happy."

I read the first page, and then I closed the journal, because I wasn't ready for more. But I brought it down with me, and now it sits on the kitchen table, next to the teacup with the chipped rim, and I look at it every time I walk by. Tomorrow, maybe, I'll read another page. Or maybe I won't. Maybe I'll just sit with the knowledge that she wanted to be remembered, that she sat in this same kitchen and tried to find words for something that resists words, and that the book is here now, waiting, patient as the house itself, for whoever is ready to hear what she had to say.

---

That's roughly 1000 words, written as a continuous meditation on returning to a family home after loss, with a particular focus on memory, presence, and the objects that outlive us.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Rain against the window. Not heavy, not light, just rain doing what rain does—falling in a way that makes you think about falling, about all the things that descend whether we notice them or not. I have a thousand words, which feels like both a lot and nothing at all. A thousand words is a short story, a long complaint, a love letter, a grocery list with annotations. A thousand words is the distance between saying something and saying everything, and there's a strange kind of freedom in knowing you can't say everything, so you just say what comes.

What comes? The smell of bread from somewhere I can't identify. The way my left knee clicks when I stand. The fact that I've been staring at this same sentence for longer than the sentence deserves, and yet the sentence doesn't seem to mind. Sentences are patient like that. They wait the way cats wait—appearing indifferent, secretly aware of every movement in the room.

I used to keep a journal. I had seventeen of them by the time I stopped. Seventeen notebooks filled with observations, complaints, small joys, the names of people I loved and then didn't. I burned them, or rather, I put them in the recycling bin over the course of several weeks, and I don't know if the recycling company actually recycled them or if they ended up in a landfill somewhere, slowly decomposing in a dark pit, and somehow that feels more honest than burning would have. A landfill is where most of our words end up anyway. The things we say to each other in airports, in cars, in the small hours when we can't sleep. Most of it just falls away, becomes soil, becomes nothing.

But some words stick. Some words get under your skin and stay there, like splinters, like songs, like the names of your children (if you have them) or the names of the children you didn't have (if you didn't). I think about that a lot. The roads not taken. The thousand words I could write versus the thousand words I'm writing. There's a poem by Robert Frost, and I can only remember the famous part, the part everyone remembers, but there's more to it, and I think the rest is about the difference between two forests and how one forest is going to matter more, somehow, to whoever walks there later. Or something like that. I might be wrong. I've been wrong about a lot of things.

The rain has stopped. I didn't notice when. The window is wet and the world outside has that freshly-washed look, the kind of clarity that only lasts until someone drives past and kicks up some dust. Everything in life is temporary. That's not a sad thought, exactly. It's just a fact, like gravity, like the number of bones in your body, like the fact that I just used the word "bones" and now you're thinking about bones, about your skeleton, about the strange architecture that holds you up.

I had a friend once who said that writing was just a way of organizing fear. I disagreed at the time, but I think he might have been right. Most of the things I've written, in the end, were just attempts to put things in order, to make sense of the disorder, to draw little boxes around the chaos and pretend the boxes held something solid. They don't. They never did. But we keep drawing them anyway, because what's the alternative? The alternative is to stand in the middle of the mess and let it wash over you, and some people can do that, and I admire them, but I'm not one of them. I'm a boxer, a labeler, a maker of lists.

Here's a list: things I know for sure. Water is wet. Time moves forward. I am sitting at a desk. The desk is made of wood. The wood came from a tree. The tree was alive once, and now it's a desk, and I'm sitting at it, and the tree is holding me up, and there's something strange and beautiful about that, the way dead things hold up living things, the way words hold up thoughts, the way a thousand words can hold up a writer, briefly, before they let go.

I've been writing for a while now, I think. I haven't counted. I should count, maybe, but counting would take me out of the flow, and the flow is where the good stuff happens, or so the writers say, the ones who teach writing workshops, the ones who have made an art of talking about writing instead of doing it. I used to teach a writing workshop. I was terrible at it. I told my students to write what they knew, and they wrote what they knew, and it was almost always terrible, and I told them it was good, and some of them believed me, and some of them didn't, and the ones who didn't went on to become better writers than I ever was, which is probably how it should be.

The light is changing. Late afternoon, the kind of light that makes everything look like a painting, or a memory of a painting, or a memory of a memory. I have a thousand words, and I've used some of them, and I have some left, and I don't know what to do with them, so I'll just keep going, the way rivers keep going, the way thoughts keep going, the way this sentence keeps going even though it has no clear destination.

I think about my grandmother sometimes. She didn't write much. She didn't read much, either, though she could read fine. She just preferred to talk, to tell stories, to weave the day into something larger than itself. She would sit in her chair and talk, and we would listen, and the stories weren't about anything, really, but they were about everything, and they're gone now, all of them, every single one, because she didn't write them down and we didn't write them down and now she's gone and the stories are gone with her. That's the thing about not writing things down. They die with you. They become ghosts that haunt no one.

I'm not saying this to make you feel guilty. I'm saying it because I'm sitting at a desk and I have words and I can put them down, and I'm doing it, and that feels like a small act of defiance against the dark, against the forgetting, against the great silence that waits for all of us. A thousand words is a small thing. But small things add up. Small things are the only things that add up, in the end.

The light is fading now. I should stop soon. But I'll write a few more, because I can, because I want to, because the rain might come back, because the light might change again, because I'm here and you're there and for a brief moment we're both somewhere else, in this place that only exists when words are being read and written, this place that is built and rebuilt every time someone picks up a pen or a keyboard, this place that is no place and every place, this place that I'm going to leave now, with a few words left over, and that's okay, that's fine, that's the way it always is, the way it always has been, the way it always will be.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The clock on the wall ticks with patient indifference, marking seconds I cannot feel. Outside, rain has begun to fall—slow at first, then with increasing conviction, as if the sky has finally decided to commit to something it had been considering for hours. I watch the droplets race down the windowpane, each one following a path no other drop has taken, writing ephemeral messages in a language I will never learn to read.

There is a particular quality to indoor air on rainy afternoons. It thickens. It settles into corners and pools on surfaces like spilled honey, carrying with it the scent of old books and dust motes dancing in grey light. The room I sit in has become a small universe, self-contained, breathing its own atmosphere. I am both observer and participant, watching myself watch the rain, and finding in that recursive gaze something almost like peace.

Words come to me in fragments. Shards of sentences, half-formed thoughts that dissolve before I can catch them. *The way light bends around a curve. The weight of a held breath. Why do we name colors after things that aren't them—navy, cyan, magenta?* These are not ideas so much as sensations, the mental equivalent of weather, passing through without asking permission.

I think about my grandmother, who died three years ago last Tuesday. She used to make tea in a chipped blue cup, and the chip was always turned toward her so I would never see it. When I think of her now, I see her hands more than her face—those hands that braided my hair with such fierce tenderness, that kneaded bread as if working prayers into the dough. I wonder if she knew, in those last months, that I would remember her this way. I wonder if it would have mattered.

A car passes on the street below, its headlights briefly smearing across the wet asphalt before disappearing around the corner. The sound of its tires on water is a small, familiar music. I have heard it a thousand times, and yet each time it seems to say something slightly different. Tonight it says: *someone is going somewhere. Someone is always going somewhere.*

My coffee has gone cold. I have been ignoring it for the past twenty minutes, and now it sits beside me like a small forgotten companion, patient and uncomplaining. I take a sip anyway. The bitterness has mellowed into something almost sweet, a taste I would not have chosen but have learned to accept. There is a metaphor there, probably, about how we change, about how the things we reject at one moment might become bearable, even welcome, in another. But I resist the metaphor. Some things are just cold coffee.

The rain continues. It has been raining for so long now that it has become the texture of silence itself, a constant, gentle percussion that fills the spaces between other sounds. I think about how water has shaped this world—carved valleys, worn mountains into sand, carried seeds across continents to places they could not otherwise reach. There is a kind of optimism in that, or maybe a kind of faith. The seed does not know where the river will take it. It only knows to release.

I have been trying to write something for weeks now. An essay, maybe, or a letter, or simply a sentence that might contain whatever it is I have been feeling. But every time I sit down, the words scatter like startled birds. I chase them across the page, and they lead me to nowhere. I begin to think that the thing I am trying to say might not be a thing that can be said. That it exists only in the attempt, in the reaching, in the way my hand hovers over the keyboard without quite touching it.

Perhaps that is enough. Perhaps the reaching is the point.

Outside, a dog barks at something I cannot see—another dog, perhaps, or a shadow, or a thought it cannot quite catch. The sound is lonely and assertive at once, a small declaration of existence in a world that mostly does not notice dogs at all. I feel a sudden kinship with it. I too am barking at things I cannot name, making noise to prove to myself that I am here, that I am here, that I am here.

The light is changing now. The rain has softened the afternoon into something approaching evening, though the clock insists it is still afternoon. I do not argue with the clock. The clock is, after all, only telling time the way time asked to be told. We are all just reporting on things we did not design.

I think I will make another cup of tea. Not coffee—tea this time, in a different cup, one without a chip. I will hold it with both hands and feel the warmth seep into my palms, and I will watch the rain some more, and I will not try to write anything at all. Sometimes the bravest thing is to stop reaching. Sometimes the seed needs to rest before it can root.

The dog has stopped barking. The rain continues.

So do I.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Here is a stream-of-consciousness piece of writing, exactly one thousand words long, unfiltered and unedited:

I woke up this morning thinking about the color of Tuesday. It's a strange thought, I know, but sometimes the mind wanders to peculiar places before the sun has fully committed to the day. Tuesday, in my mind, is a pale lavender, the kind of color you see in old photographs where everything has been bleached by time and memory. It's neither warm nor cold, just there, hovering in the background of ordinary existence.

The coffee machine is making its usual gurgling protest, a sound I've come to associate with the beginning of my waking hours. There's something almost philosophical about the way it sputters and sighs, as if it too dreads the responsibilities of the day. I poured the dark liquid into a chipped mug, one of three remaining from a set I bought years ago when I had different expectations about who I'd become. The other two broke in ways I don't remember anymore, which is probably for the best.

Outside, the neighborhood is doing what neighborhoods do. Dogs are being walked by people who look like they would rather be anywhere else. Cars are starting and stopping in the eternal dance of suburban commuting. A neighbor's wind chime, the one shaped like seashells but hanging in landlocked Indiana, catches a breeze I cannot feel from my kitchen window. I wonder if the person who hung it ever thinks about the irony. Probably not. Most people don't think about irony at seven in the morning. I shouldn't either, but here I am.

My refrigerator hums a single note, almost musical, definitely persistent. It's been doing this for months now, and I've convinced myself it's a feature rather than a malfunction. The repairman I never called would probably disagree, but he doesn't live here, and I do, and the refrigerator and I have reached an understanding. It hums, I ignore it, and we both pretend this is normal.

I spent yesterday reading about octopuses, which is something I do now apparently. Three hearts, no bones, the ability to change color in milliseconds. I find this deeply unfair. Humans spend thousands of dollars on therapy, meditation retreats, and self-help books just to achieve a fraction of that kind of flexibility. An octopus just does it, casually, like changing a shirt. If I could change colors based on my mood, I suspect I'd spend most days a confused mottled grey, the color of indecision and mild existential dread.

The mailman came and went. I didn't check the mail because checking the mail requires pants, and I'm not ready to make that commitment yet. Bills, probably. Advertisements for products I don't need. Once, years ago, I received a letter from a friend who had moved away, and it made the entire ritual worthwhile. Now it's mostly just paper and disappointment. Still, I should check eventually. The box is probably getting full, a small cardboard monument to my avoidance.

There's a spider in the corner of the ceiling that I've been watching for three days. I've named it Gerald, which feels like a significant commitment to something I might have to kill eventually. Gerald doesn't seem to be doing much. Sometimes he moves an inch to the left, sometimes an inch to the right, but mostly he just hangs there, existing in the particular way that spiders exist. I respect that. I'm not sure I could hang from a ceiling for three days straight without questioning my life choices, but Gerald seems to have made peace with it.

I wonder about the people who lived in this house before me. Did they stand in this same kitchen, looking out this same window, drinking from similar mugs, contemplating similar spiders? Did they feel the same particular blend of contentment and restlessness that I feel most mornings? The walls have absorbed so many moments, so many ordinary Tuesdays, and they'll absorb mine too, eventually, without comment or judgment.

The light is changing now. Morning is transitioning into something more committed, the sun finally clearing the neighbor's roof and streaming through the window in a way that makes everything look slightly more real. My coffee is half gone and cooling. Gerald is still on the ceiling. The refrigerator hums its single persistent note. The world continues its rotation, indifferent to my observations of it, carrying me along whether I'm ready or not.

I should do something productive today. There are lists I've made and forgotten, goals I've set and abandoned, versions of myself I've imagined and failed to become. But for now, for this particular moment, I'm just here, in this kitchen, drinking cooling coffee, watching a spider, being thoroughly, completely, unremarkably alive. And maybe that's enough. Maybe that's the whole point I've been missing all along. Just to be here, in this body, in this room, on this Tuesday that's almost the color of lavender.

The coffee is cold now. I'll make another cup.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Here's a free write:

The coffee shop on the corner has been there for as long as I can remember, though the name has changed three times. First it was called The Drowsy Spoon, then it became Lucky Beans, and now it goes by something in French that no one can pronounce correctly. The owner changes but the windows stay the same—those wide, smudged panes that let in slants of morning light and make everything inside look slightly underwater.

I go there most days around 4 PM, which is that strange hour when the morning rush has long since cleared out and the evening crowd hasn't yet arrived. The baristas know me by the cup I always choose, a chipped ceramic thing with a faded blue rim that I brought from home. They fill it without asking now, a small kindness that has accumulated over months into something that feels like friendship, though I don't know their names and they don't know mine.

Outside, the city does what cities do. It breathes and complains and carries on. A woman walks her dog past the window every Tuesday, a small terrier with a red bandana. A man in a green coat stands at the bus stop across the street, checking his phone with the intensity of someone waiting for important news. The light changes. A pigeon lands on the awning. The pigeon leaves. The light changes again.

I used to think I needed to do something significant with my hours, to make them count in some measurable way. Now I sit here and watch the light move across the floor and I think maybe this is enough. Maybe counting is overrated. The coffee is warm in my hands. The chair is old and holds the shape of everyone who has ever sat in it. Somewhere, a milk pitcher is being steamed, and the sound of it is the most comforting sound I know.

There is a crack in the ceiling that looks like a river, or maybe a branch, or maybe nothing at all—just a crack in a ceiling, doing what cracks do. I've been studying it for weeks. It hasn't changed, but I have. Yesterday it looked like fear. Today it looks like a path.

Outside, the seasons are turning, though I couldn't tell you exactly when the shift happened. The trees on the block have started giving up their leaves, one by one, in a slow and unhurried surrender. I find this unbearably beautiful, though I couldn't explain why. A leaf falls. It is not special. It is the most special thing in the world.

I think about time a lot these days. How it doesn't pass so much as accumulate, layer upon layer, like dust on a bookshelf or snow on a windowsill. We are all of us walking through our own weather, carrying our private climates. The woman with the dog is probably thinking about dinner. The man at the bus stop is probably in love with someone, or grieving someone, or both. The pigeon, if pigeons think at all, is probably just happy to be a pigeon.

My coffee is almost gone. I'll order another one soon, or maybe I'll go home. The light is doing something interesting now, falling through the window at an angle that turns the whole room golden for about three minutes. I've started timing it. Three minutes, give or take, depending on the weather. Tomorrow it will be the same, and different, and I will be here to see it, or I won't, and that will be okay too.

The bell above the door jingles. Someone new walks in, shaking off the cold, and the whole room rearranges itself slightly to make room for them. I watch them order, watch them find a seat, watch them look around with that particular expression people have when they're deciding whether to stay or go. They stay.

I smile into my empty cup. There are still a thousand things I haven't said, but for now, the afternoon is enough. For now, the light is enough. For now.
